sources.text: Binary search requires a sorted array. Use the half-open interval [lo, hi): lo is included and hi is excluded. Initialize lo to zero and hi to the array length.

While lo is less than hi, set mid to lo plus floor((hi - lo) / 2). If array[mid] equals the target, return mid. If array[mid] is smaller, set lo to mid + 1. Otherwise set hi to mid. If the loop ends without a match, return -1.
Find 12 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16]. With lo = 0 and hi = 5, mid = 2 gives 8, so lo becomes 3. Next mid = 4 gives 16, so hi becomes 4. Next mid = 3 gives 12. Return index 3.

With constant-time array indexing, worst-case search time is O(log n), because each iteration roughly halves the interval. This iterative version uses O(1) auxiliary space. Sorting cost is excluded from that search-only runtime.
Duplicates are allowed, but this version does not promise the first occurrence. For the exam, keep track of whether hi is included or excluded.
The invariant written on the board explains why those updates are safe. I am pointing to the proof here, but I am not reading it aloud.

key_points.description: Sorted-input precondition and half-open boundary convention.
Correct loop, midpoint, branch updates, match return, and failure return.
Worked example retains all three comparisons and intermediate bounds.
O(log n) time with constant-time indexing, halving rationale, O(1) iterative space, and sorting exclusion.
Duplicates do not imply first-occurrence guarantee.
Exam emphasis on whether hi is included or excluded.
Board proof is unavailable; no invented invariant attributed to the lecturer.

sources.text: Dijkstra's algorithm works with negative edge weights.
Correction: I misspoke. The standard Dijkstra algorithm requires nonnegative edge weights. Zero-weight edges are allowed. Do not write that negative edges are supported.
Relaxing an edge (u, v) means checking whether dist[u] + weight(u, v) is smaller than dist[v]. If it is, update dist[v] to that candidate distance and set predecessor[v] to u.
